name: Titus cut

lead: The Titus cut, or coiffure a la Titus, is a short, layered hairstyle, often with curls, that was worn by men and women in late 18th-century France and England. It broke with the big wigs and elaborate hair of the period and presented a simple, classical look.
Today the name is used for brushed-forward Roman-style cuts, which give a short, textured fringe and are used to frame the face and soften a receding hairline.

paras: A barber cuts the hair short and layered, and the top is brushed forward over the forehead, sometimes with curl or texture. Low-maintenance styling is typical.
No health risks are documented for the haircut.

lead: The Titus cut, or coiffure a la Titus, was a short, layered hairstyle, often curled, worn by men and women in late 18th-century France and England [1]. It was described as a simple, classical look that broke sharply with large wigs and elaborate styles [1].

The style is said to have been popularised in 1791 by the French actor Francois-Joseph Talma, who played Titus in a Paris production of Voltaire's Brutus [1]. Its plainness tied it to the French Revolution, and it was also called coiffure a la victime in France and coiffure a la guillotine in England [1].

A 1802 issue of the Journal de Paris reported that more than half of elegant women were wearing their hair or wigs a la Titus [1]. It fell out of fashion by the 1810s [1]. Modern brushed-forward Roman cuts draw on this classical idea.
